1:
Theophylact holds that the Lord came knowing he would be despised, so they might never say, if you had come we would have believed; and adds a second reason, that a prophet with known relations is disliked through them. A.T. Robertson denies any need to identify this visit with the earlier rejection in Luke: he was rejected both times, and a second chance for Nazareth is not incongruous. Matthew Henry notes that he had been in danger of his life there (Luke 4:29) and came again, so strangely does he wait to be gracious to enemies. John Gill supplies the timing: he entered on a common day and stayed unknown till the sabbath.

Matthew Henry observes what the townsmen conceded: the two great proofs of a divine original, the wisdom contriving his doctrine and the power ratifying it — yet, unable to deny the premises, they refused the conclusion. A.T. Robertson catches it in the tone: the question is laconic and curt, whence these things to this fellow, with a sting and a fling — they deny neither the wisdom of his words nor the wonder of his works, but felt some hocus-pocus somewhere. Charles Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts give “the many,” the majority present, and infers that since no mighty work was done at Nazareth, the works they speak of were reported from elsewhere. Adam Clarke records that several manuscripts and versions add that the astonishment was at his doctrine. Bede makes it a reproach: they despised one whom his words and deeds might have shown to be the Christ, solely on account of his kindred.

The trade divides them. John Gill reports that all the ancient copies read “the carpenter” rather than the carpenter’s son, and gives three reasons why Christ followed it — his parents’ poverty, an example of industry, and his share in the curse of eating bread by the sweat of the brow. He removes the sting by listing rabbis with trades: a shoemaker, a blacksmith, a tailor, and Hillel a hewer of wood. John Lightfoot and Adam Clarke derive it from a father’s four duties to a son — circumcise, redeem, teach the law, teach a trade — on the maxim that whoever does not teach his son to work teaches him robbery. A.T. Robertson holds both titles true, since after Joseph’s death Jesus carried on the business, and traces the word from a worker in wood to any craftsman in metal or stone, citing the ploughs and yokes an early apologist attributes to him, and calls it exaggeration to say the word throws the only flash on the first thirty years. Charles Ellicott notes that Mark alone applies the name to Christ himself; Augustine reconciles the forms, since both might be said, they believing him a carpenter because he was a carpenter’s son. John Wesley thinks he certainly wrought with his supposed father. Pseudo-Jerome allegorises: he is son of a workman whose work was the morning and the sun, the first Church and the second; and origin often brings contempt, as in the sneer, who is the son of Jesse (1 Samuel 25:10). Bede does the same, the type being complete because the Father of Christ works by fire and spirit; he adds that the brothers and sisters are relations, not sons of Joseph or Mary, as Abraham and Lot are called brothers.

On the closing verse the question is what “could not” concedes. Theophylact reads choice, not weakness: he spared them, lest unbelief before miracles earn greater blame; or else a miracle needs the recipient’s faith as well as the worker’s power. John Gill argues a Hebrew idiom, that what is not fit to be done is called impossible, and notes that Christ took his leave and was never seen there again. John Wesley gives a moral reason: more evidence would only have increased their damnation.
6:
The marvelling is taken as a real limit. John Gill calls it a surprise to Christ as man that his townsmen should reject him when they could not account for his wisdom and power on any human footing. Charles Ellicott presses further, that the word bears on the reality of the human nature and the limits within which, being truly man in spirit as well as body, he worked: whatever insight belonged to him did not exclude the wonder men feel at what comes unlooked for. A.T. Robertson balances both sides — divine insight into the heart with human limitations not clear to us — and notes that he marvelled at faith where none was expected and here at its absence where he had a right to expect it; he excuses Mary, puzzled by his recent conduct (Mark 3:21), holding there is no proof she ever lost faith. John Wesley settles it in a line: he marvelled as man, since as God nothing was strange. A.T. Robertson adds that the circuit of the villages begins a new paragraph and a third Galilean tour and belongs with the sending that follows, the verse division being a poor one. Theophylact draws the lesson from that circuit, that the Lord preached in villages as well as cities, so we should not despise little things nor seek only great ones but sow the word in lowly places.

Why they went in pairs is answered five ways. Theophylact gives two at once: a pair works more actively, two being better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9), and larger parties would not stretch to many villages. Gregory finds a moral necessity: charity has two precepts, love of God and of neighbour, and cannot exist between fewer than two, so a man without love for his neighbour should never take the office of preaching. Matthew Henry offers the rule of two witnesses and the comfort of company among strangers, every common soldier having his comrade. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke make it mutual support, Barnes adding that Christ consulted his disciples’ happiness and usefulness at once, since what makes people useful makes them happy. A.T. Robertson answers geographically, that six pairs could cover Galilee in six directions; he also defends the doubled numeral, called a Hebraism though it appears in the tragedians, the papyri and modern Greek, as vernacular Mark preserves better than the others.

On the commission itself, John Gill distinguishes the calling and ordaining, already done, from the public sending now begun, and Matthew Henry makes a rule of it: they had received that they might give and learned that they might teach, and must not always be studying in the academy when they might be preaching in the country. Charles Ellicott notes that Mark omits most of the discourse Matthew attaches to the mission, as suits a writer tracing the ministry of action rather than of speech. Bede marks the difference between giving and receiving: whatever the Lord does is done in his own power, while the disciples say instead, in the name of Jesus, arise and walk.

The catena attaches the travelling orders here, and the staff is the difficulty. Augustine harmonises by giving the word two senses: Matthew and Luke forbid even the smallest possession, while Mark permits the staff as ensign of an authority guaranteeing that nothing they leave behind will be wanting. Pseudo-Chrysostom resolves it otherwise: the stricter Gospels point to the highest perfection, while Mark speaks by permission. Bede reads the two coats as two suits of clothing, denying that a man in a land of ice and snow must go with one garment; the point is not to keep a second through anxiety. He allegorises the rest: the scrip is the burden of worldly affairs, the bread temporal delights, the money in the purse the hiding of wisdom, none of which becomes a teacher.
8:
Mark alone allows the staff, and the discrepancy is the first thing every commentator meets. A.T. Robertson sets out the options without choosing: that Mark preserves the saying more clearly than Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3, that the stricter Gospels forbid only a second staff, or that they report an early exaggeration of the sternness of the command; and he lets stand the judgment that going without even a staff is the ideal of austere simplicity. Charles Ellicott takes the simplest of these, that Matthew’s plural means they were to carry one and no more. John Wesley puts the same reading as a rule about provision: the man who had a staff might take it, but the man who had none was not to get one. Adam Clarke offers two possibilities: a single staff to each pair for carrying clothes stripped off in the heat, or, more probably, that the instruction means only that they were to leave at once as they stood and trust the rest to Providence.

The other items are handled as points of dress and custom. John Gill holds that sandals differed from shoes and were fitter for travel, so were permitted where shoes were forbidden, though he reports the contrary opinion that there was no difference and that Matthew forbids a second pair. A.T. Robertson leans that way: the distinction may be real, but the prohibition is probably of extra shoes, and the “two” all three Gospels attach to the coats most likely governs shoes and staff as well. Adam Clarke argues from etymology that the word is Chaldee for a light shoe, of lighter and meaner stuff than the boot, and adds that the sandal was originally a woman’s wear. John Wesley makes the contrast concrete: what Matthew forbids were short boots reaching above the mid-leg, then usual on journeys, while sandals were pieces of strong leather or wood tied under the foot. Charles Ellicott keeps to the social note, that these were the shoes of the poor, a sole fastened over the instep by thongs, the same word returning at Acts 12:8; on the money he prefers “no bronze,” taking the coins to be the small ones of Mark 12:42.

Two of them look outside the text. John Lightfoot illustrates the scrip from a rabbinic story in which Shammai came with his staff and his scrip to contend over a will — the vice-president of the Sanhedrin carrying a bag of victuals for the road, which shows what the article was and who might carry it. Albert Barnes notices instead what Mark leaves out, the command in Matthew not to go among Gentiles or Samaritans, and suggests two reasons: that Mark wrote for Gentile readers and the direction might have given needless offence, or that it was a temporary order no longer in force when he wrote.

On the purpose of the whole equipment they agree more than they differ. A.T. Robertson takes a second coat for a mark of comparative wealth and the directions as aimed against luxury in equipment and against providing what they could receive from the hospitality of others. John Wesley reads the mission as an initiation into apostolic work, the memory of how God cared for them when they went out unfurnished being an encouragement all their lives after — as Christ himself makes them use it when he asks whether they lacked anything (Luke 22:35). John Gill states the principle briefly, that they were to take nothing for the journey beyond what was expressly allowed.
10:
The two standing orders are read as manners rather than rules. A.T. Robertson takes “there abide” to forbid a restless way of moving from house to house and to require pains in the first choice, not to prohibit invitations; on the parting gesture he notes that Mark’s “for a testimony unto them” is absent from Matthew and is a dative of disadvantage carrying the force of Luke’s “against them.” Charles Ellicott and Adam Clarke both prefer the better manuscripts, whatsoever place shall not receive you; Clarke adds that the solemn clause about Sodom is missing from most chief copies and versions, is dropped by the editors, and was probably carried here from Matthew 10:15. John Gill reads the sending simply: they went out, some one way and some another, two by two, according to their instructions.

What they preached is placed differently. A.T. Robertson observes that the summons to repent was the message of the Baptist and of Jesus alike (Mark 1:15). Charles Ellicott makes the continuity the point: their work carried on the Baptist’s, announcing the kingdom with repentance as its one adequate preparation and baptism as its outward token, but not yet proclaiming their Master as being himself the Christ. Albert Barnes gives the grounds of the summons rather than its genealogy — sin is evil, the Messiah has come to preach forgiveness to the penitent, and at his presence the nation ought to turn. John Calvin draws a limit from the narrative: since they went through the towns and returned shortly to their Master, the office conferred at this point was temporary and lasted only a few days.

The anointing with oil is the disputed detail, and the division is sharp. John Calvin refuses any medical sense: some learned men take it for a medicine, and oil was in common use, but nothing is more unreasonable than to suppose the apostles used ordinary remedies, which would only obscure the miracles; they had been taught no art of healing, so the oil was a visible token of spiritual grace. John Lightfoot takes the opposite ground: among the Jews such anointing really was physical, though it did not always succeed, whereas the apostles’ always did; he cites the rabbi who allowed the sick to be anointed on the sabbath but would not have it done to himself, and concludes that on this footing nothing is obscure in James 5:14, where prayer is joined to the ordinary means. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke hold the middle from the other side: the practice was medical among the Jews, oil being used even on wounds (Luke 10:34), but here need not be medicinal at all, since in cases already miraculous it could avail no more than the laying on of hands and served as a sign of the comfort asked of God. Charles Ellicott keeps both halves, calling it an outward sign that showed the wish to heal and so helped faith, and at the same time a joining of a recognised remedy with prayer for the divine blessing. A.T. Robertson leaves it open, noting that the verb may be rendered rub as easily as anoint, that oil was the best medicine of the ancients, and that a ritual unction of the sick is first traceable in second-century practice; his summary is that we have God and medicine now as in the first century.

Two use the verse against a later sacrament. Charles Ellicott denies any affinity with extreme unction, which is scarcely administered until hope of cure is gone and was devised when the gift of healing had been withdrawn. John Wesley agrees: this was the standing means of healing long before extreme unction was heard of, the one used for health and the other only when life is despaired of, and the healing came not by the oil but by the blessing of God.
14:
The Gloss explains the placing: after the preaching and miracles of the disciples the evangelist fitly subjoins the report that arose among the people. Pseudo-Jerome adds why it spread, since it is not right that a candle be put under a bushel. A.T. Robertson makes the connection historically: the tour by pairs had wakened all Galilee, so the name reached even the palace — though a palace, he quotes, is late in hearing spiritual news. On the title, Pseudo-Chrysostom observes that Matthew calls him tetrarch and Luke has him ruling a fourth of his father’s kingdom, the Romans having divided it at the elder Herod’s death, while Mark calls him king either after his father’s style or because it suited his wish; John Gill agrees that courtiers and common people might so call him though he was only tetrarch. Adam Clarke notes a textual addition, that a group of manuscripts supply “his fame” as the object, which seems needed to complete the sense.

What the popular guesses conceded is weighed differently. Bede turns them into an indictment: they believed that John, who did no miracle, could rise without a single witness, while of Jesus, approved by signs and his resurrection preached by angels and apostles and men and women, they preferred to believe the body stolen. Yet he grants that in saying mighty works were therefore wrought in John they had just thoughts of the power of the resurrection, since risen men will have far greater power than while weighed down by the flesh. Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the guess “a prophet” as a veiled confession: they meant the prophet promised to Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), and were right, but feared to say plainly that this was the Christ, so they borrowed the voice of Moses to cover their surmise from their rulers. Matthew Henry is harsher: men free of the townsmen’s prejudice would still believe anything rather than the truth; and where there is an idle faith there is commonly a working fancy, since a prophet risen to do mighty works was thought neither impossible nor improbable and readily suspected when untrue, yet obstinately denied when it was true of Christ. A.T. Robertson notes what all sides granted, that miraculous powers were at work whatever the explanation, and that they differed only about the person.

Whether Herod believed his own words is the sharpest question. Augustine works it through the parallels: Luke supports Mark so far as that others, not Herod, first said John was risen, and shows Herod hesitating, so that afterwards he must have confirmed in his own mind what others said, since Matthew has him telling his servants that this is John risen — or else the words are still those of a doubting man, Mark’s report being readable either way. Pseudo-Chrysostom takes them for irony outright. Theophylact takes them at face value, that Herod, knowing he had killed a just man without cause, supposed he had risen and had received through the resurrection the power of working miracles. A.T. Robertson puts it psychologically, that superstition and a guilty conscience raised this ghost to plague him, and calls the clause about the powers a snatch of Herod’s own theology — John wrought no miracles (John 10:41), but risen he perhaps could.

Charles Ellicott supplies an illustration none of the others attempt, from a Roman satirist describing the feast of Herod’s birthday keeping a guest in superstitious fear amid lamps and violets and wine, moving his lips without speaking and seeing dark spectres of the dead. So minute a scene, he argues, must have been drawn from an actual incident rather than invented as a picture of Jewish superstition in Roman society; and he conjectures a link with the journey Antipas made to Rome at the prompting of Herodias to seek the title of king, which ended in his deposition and exile.
15:
John Gill offers two accounts of the cry that it was Elijah — that many Jews expected the Tishbite in person before the Messiah, or that Herod’s courtiers said it to divert their master from a notion that distressed him — preferring the first. John Wesley reads the third guess high: a prophet not inferior to the ancient prophets. Adam Clarke settles the wording instead: the connecting word is omitted by a very large body of manuscripts and versions and by the editors, and dropping it mends the sense. John Wesley and A.T. Robertson mark how little the debate moved Herod: he heard the various judgments and still said it was John. A.T. Robertson presses the psychology: his fears got the better of him and he settled on this nightmare, still seeing in dreams the charger with the head coming toward him; the late verb means to cut off the head, and in using it Herod acknowledges his guilt.

Mark then goes back to the death itself. A.T. Robertson notes that the narrative is little out of chronological order, the news from the fortress having perhaps arrived at the close of the Galilean circuit and ended it. On the charge, Theophylact and Bede give different grounds for one verdict: Theophylact allows the law commanded marriage to a brother’s widow, but only where he died childless, and here a daughter survived; Bede rests on the rule that a man might not marry his brother’s wife while the brother lived. Bede adds the woman’s motive, that Herodias feared Herod might repent, be reconciled to his brother, and dissolve the marriage.

The banquet is a study in weakness. Theophylact measures the fury of lust by what it displaced — Herod had such awe of John that he forgot it all to serve his fornication — and says that during the feast Satan danced in the person of the damsel, while the woman asked the head that very hour for fear her husband should repent; no longer his own master, he kept the oath and killed a just man, when it were better to break the oath than commit so great a sin. Bede agrees the oath does not excuse the murder, and observes that the only men recorded as keeping their birthdays with festive joy are Herod and Pharaoh, each staining the day with blood — Herod the more wickedly, killing the guiltless teacher of truth at a dancing girl’s asking. Remigius makes a rule of it: a lustful will drove him against a man he knew to be just, so a lesser fault became the cause of a greater, as when it is said, he that is filthy, let him be filthy still (Revelation 22:11). The Gloss fills in Herod’s better side: he feared John because he revered him as just toward men and holy toward God, and kept Herodias from killing him, doing many things because he thought John spoke by the Spirit of God and hearing him gladly as profitable.

Gregory raises the hardest question, why the greatest born of women should be imprisoned by wicked men and beheaded for a girl’s dancing. He rejects the idea that a fault was being wiped away — how should a man sin in eating whose food was locusts and wild honey, or offend in conversation who never left the wilderness? — and answers that God sinks lowest those he means to raise highest, throwing them among things despised because he draws them up to things incomprehensible; each may infer what those will suffer whom he rejects, if he so grieves those he loves. Pseudo-Jerome reads it allegorically instead: the head of the law, which is Christ, is cut from the body of the Jewish people and given to a Gentile damsel, the Roman Church, who gives it to her adulterous mother the synagogue, who will believe at the last.
18:
The ground of the rebuke is stated exactly. John Gill has John speaking to Herod in person, telling him plainly of his sin and alleging that what he had done was against the law of God. A.T. Robertson supplies the statute and its limit: the prohibition covers a brother’s wife while the brother is alive (Leviticus 18:16), whereas after a brother’s death it was often a duty to marry his widow — which is why the charge turned on the fact that Philip still lived.

Herodias is described in the same terms by all of them and with very different force. John Gill has her conceive wrath and bear an inward grudge, lying in wait for the first opportunity. Charles Ellicott prefers “had a grudge” or spite to the older rendering of a quarrel. A.T. Robertson renders the idiom in the vernacular as having it in for him, calls it a dative of disadvantage, and finds the imperfect exactly right for a woman’s standing hostility toward an upstart prophet of the wilderness who had dared to denounce her private relations: she never let up but bided her time. On the clause that she could not, he adds the distinction that the power was wanting and not the will, and that it means not yet. Adam Clarke notes only that some copies read that she sought to kill him.

What held her back is where the entry divides. John Gill allows two senses of Herod’s fear, that he had a great veneration for John or, as some understand it, a dread of him; and he brings in the other fear from Matthew, that Herod dreaded the multitude, who held John for a prophet, and would not let Herodias kill him lest the people rise. Charles Ellicott takes the word rendered “observed him” to mean that Herod had a certain reverence for his prisoner, the parallel use at Luke 2:19 being decisive for the sense; and he notes that the two adjectives divide between them righteousness as seen toward men and the same character as seen toward God, and that this full account of Herod’s feelings is peculiar to Mark. A.T. Robertson has him vacillating between two fears, of John and of Herodias, keeping the prisoner safe from her plots — she was another Jezebel — and finds the interviews down in the prison bracing his jaded mind like a whiff of fresh air, until he saw Herodias again and was at his wits’ end, knowing himself hopelessly entangled. John Wesley reckons the imprisonment at a year and a half, with Herod sending for him at times, and turns the gladness into an epigram: delusive joy, while Herodias lay in his bosom.

The last clause is disputed as a matter of text, and the difference is not small. Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson both hold that the better manuscripts read that Herod was much perplexed rather than that he did many things, Robertson pointing out that this perplexity is the very word for a man who has lost his way. Albert Barnes keeps the older reading and builds his whole comment on it: Herod did many things but not the thing demanded of him, which was to break off from his sin, and so attempted a compromise with his conscience — treating the preacher kindly, speaking well of him, relieving his wants, and hoping that such attentions might be accepted in place of putting away the woman. He turns it on his own readers, that sinners often treat ministers kindly and hear them gladly while still unwilling to repent, expecting their kindness to stand instead of what God demands.
21:
A.T. Robertson takes the convenient day for one well appointed, the day Herodias had waited for, her plans laid to make her husband do her will without knowing he was the catspaw; he sorts the guests into the magnates of civil life, the tribunes of a thousand men, and the first men of Galilee — the court, the army and the province, as John Wesley names them. John Gill notes that the dancer is called the daughter of Herodias, not of Herod, because she was Philip’s, and gives her name as Salome. A.T. Robertson places the dance at the close of the feast, when all had drunk freely, and calls such dancing almost unprecedented for women of rank, being licentious and the work of professionals: Herodias stooped to degrade her own daughter, and the drunken tetrarch was caught by a public promise.

On the oath, A.T. Robertson notes that the girl was of marriageable age despite the diminutive, that she afterwards married Philip the tetrarch, and that the offer of half a kingdom repeats an oath sworn to Esther. Adam Clarke lingers: a noble price for a dance, and such extravagance still has full scope in the east, where the rich vie in gifts of money and jewels and men of fortune have ruined themselves — one dancer gaining such ascendancy over an emperor that he made her joint governess of the empire.

Why the woman wanted this death is disputed. John Calvin rejects the guess of revenge: it was dread of being cast off, and she hoped the crime would bind Herod closer, the disgrace of a pretended marriage washed out in the prophet’s blood — which shows the anxiety of a bad conscience, since she could have barred every man from his cell and still had no rest. A.T. Robertson makes it tactics rather than fear: the girl’s going out to ask proves she had not been told beforehand and was unprepared for the ghastly answer, and the haste back was calculated too, before the king’s mood could pass. John Gill explains the withdrawal, Herodias not being at the feast, women not sitting at table at such festivals; Charles Ellicott notes that the consultation is peculiar to Mark, and that the old rendering “by and by” meant forthwith. Adam Clarke adds a motive on the guests’ side: they probably joined in the request, glad to extinguish the public reprover of their vices.

Why Herod kept the oath draws three answers. John Calvin gives the vanity of kings, who will not have a word recalled, and the sharper point that the Evangelists name the guests as the reason of his grief — whence we infer that without witnesses he would not have held to the oath though he had sworn a hundred times. A.T. Robertson calls it a conflict lost: Herod was caught again between conscience and environment, and the environment stifled the conscience. John Wesley is hardest: Herod’s honour was like the conscience of the chief priests, and innocent blood wounded neither.

On the executioner, Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson both identify Mark’s Latin word, originally a sentinel and by that date a courier and often an executioner, one of the imperial bodyguard and so of Herod’s; John Lightfoot adds that the word had passed into the Aramaic paraphrase of Genesis 39:1. John Calvin weighs the closing scenes: it aggravates the crime that the head was made a matter of sport, though the Lord gives up his people to the pride of the wicked only until he shows their blood is precious (Psalm 116:15), Herodias being stripped later of wealth and title and driven into banishment. He praises the burial as an attestation of the disciples’ piety at real danger, since the honour of a tomb is nothing to the dead but is willed by God as a token of the resurrection.
30:
The Gloss marks the return to the main narrative, and Augustine settles the order: this happened after the Baptist’s passion, so what Mark relates first happened last, since these very events moved Herod to say it was John whom he had beheaded. John Gill, Albert Barnes, Adam Clarke and Charles Ellicott note the reassembling, Clarke placing it at Capernaum Ellicott observing that Luke records the return where Matthew does not. A.T. Robertson keeps to the manner of the telling, the vivid present and the aorist that sums up their whole first tour without him, and adds that Jesus listened to it all, deeply concerned in the outcome. Bede notices who else reported: not the apostles only, but John’s disciples, telling what their own master had suffered while the Twelve were away. Matthew Henry turns the reporting into a rule: ministers are accountable for what they do and teach, and must watch over their own souls and for others as men who must give account (Hebrews 13:17) — let them neither do nor teach what they would not have repeated to the Lord Jesus. Theophylact draws it from the other end: a man sent on a mission should not go far off nor overstep his office but return often to the sender and report all he has done and taught, since we are to act and not only teach.

Why he took them apart is answered several ways. Theophylact makes it a precedent for office-holders, that those who labour in any work or in the word deserve rest and should not labour continually, and reads the withdrawal itself as humility. A.T. Robertson makes it plain necessity, they being overwrought and excited, and calls occasional change one of the needed lessons for all preachers — even Jesus felt the need of it. Adam Clarke puts it bluntly: rest is necessary for those who labour, and a zealous preacher will want it as often as a galley slave. Albert Barnes reads the coming and going as a measure of the throng that made rest impossible. Pseudo-Jerome gives a mystical reason, that the Lord took apart those he had chosen so that, living among evil men, they might not set their minds on evil, as Lot in Sodom, Job in Uz, Obadiah in the house of Ahab; and the rest of the saints here is little, their labour long. Bede adds a purpose aimed at the crowd rather than the Twelve: by seeking a desert place he tried their faith and would see whether they cared to follow — and follow they did, not on horseback nor in carriages but labouring on foot.

The crossing and the race round the lake go in small strokes. John Wesley takes the voyage across a creek or corner of the lake, and Albert Barnes notes the privacy was intended but did not hold. Charles Ellicott finds the contrast pointed in the wording, disciples by boat and crowds by land; A.T. Robertson has them refusing to be outdone, running round the head of the lake and waiting when the boat came in. Adam Clarke stops to say that scarcely a verse in the New Testament has suffered so much from transcribers, the readings being so many that one can hardly tell the original state.

What the crowd lacked comes last. A.T. Robertson argues that the want was teaching and not healing, since a crowd vigorous enough to run round the lake would have few sick, and that they had official leaders in plenty who were spiritually blind leaders of the blind. Albert Barnes says the same of the priests and scribes, proud and corrupt and neglecting the common people. Theophylact makes the figure sharper: the Pharisees were ravening wolves who devoured the sheep instead of feeding them, so the flock gathered to the true Shepherd, who gave them the word of God for food.
35:
A.T. Robertson notes that the word means daytime and much of it was gone, so the scene falls after three in the afternoon, the first evening, sunset being the second; Albert Barnes says the day was nearly done, Charles Ellicott that the same Greek word stands in both halves of the clause, John Gill that the time had gone in teaching and healing. Bede takes the failing day for more than a note of time: the Saviour refreshes the hungry at the day’s decline because, now that the end of the world draws on, or the Sun of justice has set for us in death, we are saved from wasting away in spiritual hunger.

Why they were told to feed the crowd is answered three times over. Theophylact credits them with a growth in love, pitying the multitude and interceding, then says the Lord tried them, to see whether they knew his power sufficient; their answer shows they were troubled. John Gill makes it a trial of faith that made way for the miracle, and Bede gives the evidential version, that they were called to break bread so that they might testify they had none and the miracle be better known. He adds that in calling them so the Lord intimates how our hungry souls are fed daily by them, by their letters and examples.

Who actually spoke is disputed. Augustine notes that John assigns the objection to Philip while Mark gives it to the disciples, and resolves it by making Philip the mouthpiece of the rest, or by the habit of putting a plural for a singular; the same holds for the loaves, which John credits to Andrew. A.T. Robertson works from the fuller account: Jesus asked Philip what food there was, and when the disciples protested told them to go and see how many loaves they could find, whereupon Andrew reported the lad — and John alone tells of the boy and the lunch his mother had given him.

The two hundred pence are valued two ways. John Lightfoot treats it as proverbial rather than calculated, showing that the coin equals the rabbinic zuz and that two hundred is a famous number in the rulings, fixed as a woman’s portion and as the fine for a blow on the cheek, so it came readily to the disciples’ lips. Albert Barnes takes it for a real reckoning, about six pounds, and thinks the common purse held near that sum, so Philip asked with wonder whether they should spend their whole property on one meal, implying it were better to dismiss the crowd. A.T. Robertson agrees it was probably all they had with them or more. On smaller words, Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson both prefer farms to country for the scattered holdings, Ellicott noting that the better manuscripts shorten the request to buying themselves something to eat, Robertson that the villages may have included the northern Bethsaida.

The numbers draw out the allegorists, and one refuses. Bede makes the five loaves the books of Moses and the two fishes the Psalms and Prophets. Gregory reads the ranks as the churches making up the one Catholic Church, and finds the Jubilee rest in fifty, which must be doubled to reach a hundred — the first step being to rest from doing evil and the further one from evil thoughts, so some lie down in fifties and others in hundreds. Pseudo-Jerome takes the twelve baskets for the thrones on which the apostles will judge the tribes when the remnant of Israel is saved. Augustine declines all this and treats the seating as a harmony question: Luke gives fifties and Mark hundreds and fifties, one mentioning a part and the other the whole, so Mark fills up what Luke leaves out and nothing need perplex us. Theophylact keeps to the Greek, noting that the phrase rendered by companies is doubled there.
39:
The seating is the part Mark tells most vividly, and the commentators dwell on it. John Gill notes that with no tables or couches the people were simply directed to recline as they would at a meal. Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson both observe that the Greek expresses distribution by plain repetition — companies and companies — instead of the usual particles, Robertson adding that the word first meant a drinking party and then any party of guests, and that the groups may have been arranged like tables open at one end.

What the word for “ranks” pictures divides them. John Gill and John Lightfoot look to the rabbinic schools: Gill says the form was that of little beds in a garden or rows of vines in a vineyard, which is how the scholars of the wise men sat, and Lightfoot supplies the technical phrase rank by rank and the school at Jabneh, celebrated as the vineyard in Jabneh precisely because its scholars sat in rows like a vineyard planted rank by rank. Albert Barnes and Charles Ellicott keep to the garden itself, Ellicott noting that the primary sense is a bed of flowers or herbs and that the reduplication paints the whole scene to the eye. A.T. Robertson completes the picture with the colour: half-reclining in their many-coloured clothes, the groups looked like garden beds with orderly walks between the rows, and there was colour as well as order in the grouping. He also draws a chronological inference from the grass, which is green in that country mainly at passover, so that the notice here implies a ministry longer than a single year.

Whether the arithmetic works is a second question. John Wesley sets it out, fifty in rank and a hundred in file, so that a hundred multiplied by fifty makes just five thousand. Adam Clarke reports that reckoning and objects to it on practical grounds: if they sat fifty deep, how could the disciples conveniently serve them with the bread and the fish? Albert Barnes avoids the difficulty by loosening the numbers, since we need not suppose the companies exactly formed or arranged, the expression being a way of indicating a multitude. Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson both point out that the count is of men in the strict sense, excluding women and children.

The blessing and the fragments draw shorter notes. Adam Clarke argues that the word God should be supplied as the object of the blessing, since the food we receive from him is already blessed and does not need blessing from man, while the giver deserves our warmest thanks as often as we partake of his bounty. A.T. Robertson observes that the fishes appear to have been in excess of the twelve baskets of broken bread, and notes that the Greek has two different words for basket in these narratives. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke both suppose the baskets to have belonged either to the disciples, who carried their provisions in them, or to people in the crowd, Clarke suggesting that some had brought them to carry things for the sick.

On the miracle itself the two grammarians are the most emphatic. Adam Clarke notes that the qualifying word “about” is dropped by a great majority of the best manuscripts and by the editors, and calls this one of the most astonishing of the miracles, one that could not be counterfeited and a full proof of the divinity of Christ. A.T. Robertson calls it a nature miracle that only God can work, dismisses any explanation by the accelerating of natural processes, and rests the case on the witnesses: the record of Matthew, the eyes of Peter behind Mark, and the testimony of the beloved disciple, which he calls overwhelming evidence.
45:
The Gloss reads the two miracles as a pair of claims: by the loaves he showed himself Creator of the world, by the walking that his body was free of the weight of sin, by stilling the wind that he was Master of the elements. Why he had to constrain the disciples is answered two ways. Pseudo-Chrysostom says they could not part from him without pain, from affection and from not knowing how he would rejoin them; John Wesley says simply that they did not care to go without him. A.T. Robertson supplies a harder reason: the crowds were in the mood to start a revolution and proclaim him king, and the disciples were in danger of being swept into the Pharisaic conception of the kingdom, defeating his whole training of them — so he forced them into the boat and stayed to persuade the crowds away, as Mark’s present tense pictures him doing. Bede cites the same: they would have taken him by force to make him king.

Where they were sent is a puzzle. Bede raises it, that Mark has them cross to Bethsaida while Luke places the feeding in its parts, and resolves it by taking Luke to mean the desert places belonging to the town rather than the country about it, Mark meaning the town. Charles Ellicott answers that there were two places of the name, and the marginal “over against Bethsaida” has nothing to warrant it, being suggested by someone unaware of the second. A.T. Robertson names them: the western Bethsaida here, Bethsaida Julias on the east. Adam Clarke brings in the third statement, that John says Capernaum, and supposes they were bidden steer for either of two places four miles apart on one shore.

The withdrawal to pray becomes instruction. Theophylact observes that prayer requires rest and silence, and Matthew Henry that Christ prayed often and long despite all his preaching, and prayed alone — an encouragement to depend on the intercession he now makes continually. Bede adds a warning: not every man who prays goes up a mountain, for he alone prays well who seeks God in prayer, while one who prays for riches or an enemy’s death sends his vile petitions up from the lowest depths. Matthew Henry notices how unwilling the fed crowd was to leave, and answers that here we have no continuing city, not even in communion with Christ, the everlasting feast being reserved for another state.

The delay on the water is deliberate. Theophylact holds that the Lord permitted the danger so they might learn patience, leaving them in it all night to teach them not to hope for help the moment tribulation begins; and even when about to end it he first increased their fear, then reassured them and stilled the tempest by entering the ship. Augustine presses the detail that he would have passed them by, inferring that he went a different way as a stranger might, since they took him for a spirit — and asks how he could wish to pass men whose fears he then quieted, unless the wish to pass was what wrung from them the cry for help. Chrysostom marks the turn: as soon as they knew his voice their fear left them; Pseudo-Jerome reads the calm allegorically, the storm ceasing when Jesus sat down, that is, reigned, in the ship, which is the Church.

On the hours, Pseudo-Chrysostom counts four watches of three hours, so the fourth falls after the ninth hour, and offers a second scheme in which the watches are the ages: to the deluge, to Moses, to the Lord’s coming, and the fourth in which he spoke to his disciples. John Gill and A.T. Robertson take the evening here for the second and later one, at sunset or after, Robertson adding that Jesus seems to have stayed some hours alone on the beach.
48:
How he saw them is asked first. John Gill allows either that he watched them with his bodily eyes from the mountain or that he knew their case by his omniscience, and John Wesley settles it the second way, since darkness could veil nothing from him. On the word for their labour, John Gill takes them to be vexed and tortured, in pain of mind as well as fatigue of body, since the boat was worked by oars and it was hard labour to keep it from being overset. A.T. Robertson traces the same word through its harder senses, from torment under examination — the papyri use it of what is done to slaves — to plain distress, and notes that the verb for rowing means literally to drive; the fourth watch falls between three and six in the morning, the wind was in their faces, and they had made so little progress that they should have been across long before.

The words about his passing them are handled cautiously. A.T. Robertson points out that this detail is in Mark alone, and that the cry which followed was literally a shriek of terror. John Wesley takes the phrase to mean not an intention to leave them but a manner of walking, as if he were passing by. Adam Clarke explains their guess about a spirit as a guess about the storm, that they took him for the one by whom it had been raised. John Gill observes what made the sight certain: had one man seen it, it might have been thought a fancy, but every one of them saw it, which is what gave them the greater concern. A.T. Robertson notes that they did not know him in the darkness and had never seen any man walk on water, so that it was his voice that reassured them.

Mark leaves out the best-known part of the story, and two of them explain why. A.T. Robertson observes that this Gospel does not give Peter’s walking and beginning to sink, and suggests that Peter was perhaps not fond of telling that story. Charles Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by a different route, holding that the Evangelist’s personal connection with the Apostle may account for the omission of a narrative of his rashness and failing faith, just as it accounts for the note about the disciples’ state of mind, which he receives as Peter’s own recollection. John Gill simply supplies the missing incident from the other Gospel, and A.T. Robertson adds that the amazement recorded instead is peculiar to Mark, the imperfect tense picturing the excited men vividly.

What the hardened heart means is the last and sharpest question. Albert Barnes is careful to deny the natural reading: it does not mean that they were opposed to Jesus or had what we call hardness of heart, but only that their minds were slow to perceive his power, the word heart being frequently used in that sense. John Wesley guards it the same way in a line, that they were not reprobates and the phrase means only that they were slow and dull of apprehension. John Gill gives the substance of the failure, that they had not attended to or learned from a miracle seen the day before which was as much an act of omnipotence as the walking or the stilling of the wind, or more so. Charles Ellicott states the inference they should have drawn, that all natural forces were subject to their Master’s sovereignty. A.T. Robertson keeps the word hard and applies it forward: their reasoning process was hardened, and there are men today of such intellectual denseness that they cannot believe God can or would work miracles, least of all miracles in nature.
53:
The Gloss marks the transition, that having shown the danger of the crossing and the deliverance from it the evangelist now names the place they reached. Adam Clarke describes the district as lying along the coast of the lake and, on the testimony of the ancient historian, exceedingly pleasant and fertile, and derives its name from words for a garden and a prince, either because a king had a garden there or from the fertility itself. A.T. Robertson takes the verb for their landing, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it is old Greek and appears in the papyri, to mean that they cast anchor or lashed the boat to a post on shore, and observes that the night wind had carried them several miles south of the place they were making for.

How they were recognised is a small disagreement. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke both take the word to mean that the people recollected him, having seen him preach and work miracles in those parts before, and A.T. Robertson renders it as knowing fully, which by now nearly everyone did. Bede allows both possibilities and prefers the first: they knew him by report rather than by his features, though the greatness of the miracles may have made his person known to some. John Gill notes that those who recognised him ran themselves and also sent messengers into every part of the district, and Bede makes that the measure of their faith, since they were not content with healing for those already present but sent round to the other towns, that all might hasten to the Physician.

The manner of the healings is described rather than explained. Theophylact observes that they did not invite him into their houses to heal them but brought the sick out to him, and traces the confidence to the report of the woman with the issue of blood, which had reached many ears and produced the great faith by which they were healed. A.T. Robertson notes the beds to be the pallets of the poor, like the one let down through the roof, and reads the imperfect tenses as continuous and repeated action, with the news travelling and the crowds running about after him; the grammar of the closing clauses, he adds, is deliberately general and indefinite, so that one must enlarge the details to get an idea of the richness of this healing ministry at the close of the Galilean work, when the excitement was at its highest pitch. Adam Clarke distinguishes the three words, the villages being small towns near the cities and the country the hamlets at a distance from them, and draws the ministerial lesson: Christ confined his ministry and his miracles to no place, and wherever he went they needed his help and had it granted immediately, which he calls a perfect pattern for every preacher of the gospel. Charles Ellicott prefers farms or hamlets for the third word and holds that the three together make almost an exhaustive list of the grades of human settlement; he would read market-places rather than streets, and hem or fringe rather than border, and notes that the Greek tense of the healing implies an event frequently recurring.

Two of the fathers turn the hem into a figure. Theophylact takes it for the slightest of the commandments, so that whoever transgresses even that is answerable, while whoever holds by it is made whole. Pseudo-Jerome reads the whole clause as a promise still outstanding, that the words about all who touched him being made whole will be fulfilled when grief and mourning shall flee away.
